Here are my verse-by-verse research notes on Deuteronomy 7, drawn strictly from the pages available through the searches and fetches above.

---

## DEUTERONOMY 7 – VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1 — “When the LORD your God brings you into the land…and He drives out before you many nations…seven nations larger and stronger than you”

- Moses says “When,” not “if.” God’s promise is certain; the conquest will happen. This is God’s faithfulness to the Abrahamic covenant and His power to complete what He has begun (cf. Philippians 1:6). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-7-commentary ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- The seven nations represent “completeness”—seven being the biblical number of fullness. Other lists in Scripture name anywhere from three to ten nations; the point is not an exhaustive ethnic catalogue but that Israel faced a full complement of foes. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-7-commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- The seven are “greater and mightier” than Israel. Humanly speaking, Israel had no chance—they were outnumbered and outgunned. God deliberately brought them to face an impossible challenge, so that victory would be unmistakably His. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- Ellicott connects this chapter to the first and second commandments: the exhortation concerns treatment of idolaters in the conquest and avoidance of any intercourse that might turn Israel from Jehovah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/7.htm

### v. 2 — “You must devote them to complete destruction. Make no treaty with them and show them no mercy.”

- The Hebrew term for “utterly destroy” is *herem* (the “ban”), meaning to dedicate something exclusively to God for destruction. It is related to the concept of holiness—something so holy it cannot be for human use and must therefore be destroyed. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-7-commentary
- The Canaanites were not destroyed arbitrarily. God had given them over 400 years to repent (Genesis 15:13–16). They knew judgment was coming (Joshua 2:9–11) yet most refused to respond in faith like Rahab or surrender like the Gibeonites. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- “No covenant” and “no mercy” are political and military absolutes. The Canaanite religious culture was so corrupt that any tolerated presence would be an irresistible temptation to Israel. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- Genesis 15:16, Numbers 33:55 and Joshua 23:13 state the theological reason for total destruction: the iniquity of the Amorite was now complete, and these nations would become a snare if spared. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html

### v. 3 — “Do not intermarry with them. Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons.”

- This command carries no racial overtones—it is entirely religious. Exodus 34:12–17 makes the same point: marriage with Canaanites would lead to idolatry. The major later passages on this are Ezra 10 and Nehemiah 13. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes this was the primary condition behind God’s prohibition of intermarriage: the inevitable pull toward other gods. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-7.html
- Constable notes that believers should not make defiling alliances with unbelievers pursuing rebellion against God, citing 2 Corinthians 6:14–18 as a parallel principle. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html

### v. 4 — “Because they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods. Then the anger of the LORD will burn against you, and He will swiftly destroy you.”

- The danger is not theoretical: foreign spouses would turn Israel’s children away from Yahweh. Numbers 33:55 and Joshua 23:13 use the identical warning. The modern Jewish concept that the mother determines legal Jewish status may originate from this principle. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- The Canaanites’ corrupt worship—involving fertility cults, sacred prostitution, and child sacrifice—presented a mortal danger to Israel’s faith. If Israel tolerated it, they would face the same destruction as the Canaanites. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- The Pulpit Commentary homiletics stresses: the alternative was “Exterminate these incorrigible sinners, or by their seductions they will lead you on to your destruction at the hands of a just God.” — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/7.htm

### v. 5 — “Tear down their altars, smash their sacred pillars, cut down their Asherah poles, and burn their idols in the fire.”

- Four specific actions: tear down altars, smash sacred pillars (phallic stone symbols of Baal, the male fertility god), cut down Asherah poles (wooden symbols of the female consort goddess), and burn carved images. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- Asherah was the mother goddess of the Canaanite pantheon, represented by an evergreen tree or pole. The cult was of the most sensual and sordid type, including sacred prostitution. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- The failure to do this completely would leave corrupting influences (as indeed happened repeatedly in Judges and Kings). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/

### v. 6 — “For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all peoples on the face of the earth.”

- “Holy” means set apart. Israel was holy in their standing before God by His choosing, before they were holy in conduct—position precedes performance. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- “Prized possession” (Hebrew *segullah*) means a people who belong to God alone, His treasured possession, like a crown jewel. It is used metaphorically of God’s covenant people (cf. Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 14:2; 26:18; Psalm 135:4). In the NT, the language is applied to the Church (Titus 2:14; 1 Peter 2:9). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-7.html
- OT election was for service to reveal God to the nations; it was not always tied to individual salvation (cf. Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28–45:1). God chose Israel to choose a nation to choose a world. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html

### vv. 7–8 — “The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous… but because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers…”

- God’s choice was entirely rooted in His own character, not in Israel’s merit. Israel was actually “the fewest of all peoples.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- The Hebrew verb for “set His love” (*ḥāšaq*) means “to bind” or “press together,” implying a deliberate attachment. God’s grace is accentuated by Israel’s lack of attractiveness—they were stiff-necked and rebellious (Deuteronomy 9:6, 13). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- Two reasons are given for God’s choice: (1) His love, and (2) His covenant oath to the patriarchs. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-7.html
- “Redeemed” (*pādâ*) means “to buy with a price”—used of buying a slave out of bondage. The Exodus is the supreme OT act of redemption and the foundation of Israel’s obligation to obey. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html

**Denominational note (Reformed):** Constable (Dallas Seminary) stresses that Israel’s election was “due not to anything in her that merited God’s favor, but only to the free choice of God to bless whom He would bless.” This reflects the Reformed emphasis on unconditional election. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html

### vv. 9–10 — “Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion for a thousand generations… but those who hate Him He repays to their faces with destruction.”

- God is described as (1) faithful (*ne’ĕmān*, a Niphal participle meaning trustworthy), (2) covenant-keeping, and (3) abounding in *ḥesed* (loving devotion/covenant mercy). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- “To their faces” (v. 10, unique to this verse) probably means judgment falls immediately—not deferred to unborn generations, but right then and there upon those who sinned. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- The balance between God’s faithfulness to those who love Him and His swift justice against those who hate Him motivates Israel to covenant loyalty. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/

### v. 11 — “So keep the commandments and statutes and ordinances that I am giving you to follow this day.”

- This is a concluding exhortation: knowing God’s character of faithful love and certain justice, Israel should obey. The three terms (“commandments,” “statutes,” “ordinances”) cover the full scope of divine revelation given through Moses. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html

### vv. 12–13 — “If you listen to these ordinances… the LORD your God will keep His covenant… He will love you and bless you and multiply you… bless the fruit of your womb… grain, new wine, and oil…”

- The blessings are conditional (“if you listen… and keep and do them”). The Mosaic covenant has a reciprocal structure: Israel’s obedience activates the promised blessing. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- Grain, wine, and oil represent the three principal food products of Canaan (S. R. Driver). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html
- The Hebrew root *brk* (“bless”) occurs five times in vv. 12–16, emphasising that abundance is relational, not mechanistic. — https://biblehub.com/q/Deut_7_13_and_God_s_prosperity_promise.htm

**Denominational note (Word of Faith / Prosperity Gospel):** Word of Faith teachers (Kenneth Hagin, Kenneth Copeland) appeal to this passage and the Abrahamic covenant to teach that material prosperity is every believer’s covenant right. The Pneuma Review notes that this involves a “selective hermeneutic” that stacks prosperity texts while excluding passages about suffering and contentment. A reconstructed prosperity theology would devalue wealth and treat it as “merely an appendix” to the superior blessing of right relationship with God. Oral Roberts defined prosperity as having enough for oneself with surplus to help the poor. — https://pneumareview.com/reconstructing-word-of-faith-theology/

**Lutheran response (LCMS):** The LCMS rejects the teaching that God intends all His children to be rich in material possessions. The New Testament teaches that “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of possessions” (Luke 12:15). Faith is a gift worked by the Holy Spirit, not a human force by which one demands blessings. — https://files.lcms.org/api/file/preview/A810B65D-D26A-4762-8633-D85070F5E77A

**Reformed/Baptist response:** Desiring God (John Piper) calls the prosperity gospel “an idolatrous perversion of the gospel according to which Jesus is a means to God’s full blessings, primarily of wealth, health, and might.” — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-gods-of-the-prosperity-gospel

Bible.org adds that prosperity teachers ignore the second half of Galatians 3:14 (“that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith”), showing Paul was speaking of spiritual blessing, not material wealth. — https://bible.org/article/bankruptcy-prosperity-gospel-exercise-biblical-and-theological-ethics

### v. 14 — “You will be blessed above all peoples; among you there will be no barren man or woman or livestock.”

- Barrenness was considered a curse in the ancient Near East. The promise of universal fertility—human and animal—represents the fullness of covenant blessing and directly counters Canaanite fertility religion, which looked to Baal and Asherah for fertility rather than to Yahweh. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html

### v. 15 — “The LORD will remove from you all sickness. He will not lay upon you any of the terrible diseases you knew in Egypt…”

- “Terrible diseases of Egypt” is literally “the evil, malignant, or horrible diseases of Egypt.” Ancient sources confirm virulent diseases like elephantiasis, ophthalmia, and dysentery were common there. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- Dr. S. I. McMillen (*None of These Diseases*) noted that many of God’s laws had direct health benefits: circumcision, quarantine, washing in running water, and kosher dietary laws substantially reduced disease. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- These physical blessings were part of the Sinai covenant’s promises to an obedient Israel (cf. Exodus 15:26; Deuteronomy 28). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/

### v. 16 — “You must destroy all the peoples… Do not look on them with pity. Do not worship their gods, for that will be a snare to you.”

- “Snare” (*môqēš*) is literally a baited animal trap. The Canaanite gods must be completely avoided. This verse closes the blessing section by returning to the command of destruction—obedience and separation are inseparable. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- The command is repeated from v. 2: “your eye shall have no pity on them.” False pity would lead to Israel’s own destruction. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html

### vv. 17–18 — “You may say in your heart, ‘These nations are greater than we are; how can we drive them out?’ But do not be afraid…”

- “Say in your heart” is a Hebrew idiom for doubting or thinking anxiously. God anticipates Israel’s fear and answers it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- The remedy for fear is remembrance: “remember well what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and all Egypt.” Past faithfulness fuels present courage. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- Constable notes: “The Israelites could obtain encouragement in battle by remembering God’s past faithfulness.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html

### v. 19 — “The great trials that you saw, the signs and wonders, and the mighty hand and outstretched arm by which the LORD your God brought you out.”

- Five phrases describe the Exodus: (1) great trials, (2) signs, (3) wonders, (4) mighty hand, (5) outstretched arm. These all appear repeatedly in Deuteronomy as the central display of God’s redemptive power. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- David Guzik notes that in the new covenant, believers have an even greater act of redemption to remember: Christ’s death and resurrection. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/

### v. 20 — “Moreover, the LORD your God will send the hornet against them until even the survivors hiding from you have perished.”

- Two interpretations of “hornet” (*ṣir‘â*): (1) literal swarms of stinging insects that would assist Israel’s attacks (cf. Exodus 23:28; Joshua 24:12), or (2) figurative for some powerful agency God would use—perhaps an army described as a swarm of bees (cf. Deuteronomy 1:44). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/

### v. 21 — “Do not be terrified by them, for the LORD your God, who is among you, is a great and awesome God.”

- “Great and awesome” (*gādôl wĕnôrā’*) describes YHWH’s transcendent majesty. The same phrase appears in Deuteronomy 10:17, Nehemiah 1:5 and 4:14. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- “In your midst” is a profound truth: the transcendent, holy God dwells among His people (cf. Exodus 29:45; Numbers 5:3; 35:34). This is the reality behind the name “Emmanuel.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html

### v. 22 — “The LORD your God will drive out these nations before you little by little. You will not be enabled to eliminate them all at once, or the wild animals would multiply around you.”

- God would not grant instant, total victory. The reason given is practical and merciful: if the land were suddenly depopulated, wild beasts would overrun it before Israel was numerous enough to manage it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html
- Spiritually, God often works “little by little” in the believer’s life. Instant victory might seem easier, but God prioritises growth in the process of possessing what He has given. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- Under Joshua it took about seven years to conquer the main strongholds (Joshua 11:18). After that, individual tribes were responsible to drive out remaining pockets. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/

### vv. 23–24 — “But the LORD your God will give them over to you and throw them into great confusion, until they are destroyed. He will hand their kings over to you…”

- God’s method: He would throw the Canaanites into “great confusion” (*mĕhûmâ gĕdōlâ*), a phrase evoking the holy-war panic by which God routed enemies (cf. Exodus 23:27; Joshua 10:10). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html
- The promise extends to the kings: their very names would be wiped from under heaven—complete obliteration of political as well as religious power. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/

### v. 25 — “You must burn up the images of their gods; do not covet the silver and gold that is on them or take it for yourselves…”

- Some ancient idols were plated with gold and silver. The monetary value and craftsmanship could tempt Israelites to keep them, leading remotely at least to idolatry. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- The whole idol was under the ban (*herem*). Precious metals were not to be kept for personal use. Constable notes they were to be destroyed or brought to the tabernacle as dedicated to God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html
- The verb “covet” (*ḥāmad*) is the same as in the Tenth Commandment (Deuteronomy 5:21), linking the prohibition to the Decalogue. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/

### v. 26 — “You must not bring any detestable thing into your house, or you, like it, will be set apart for destruction. You are to utterly detest and abhor it, because it is set apart for destruction.”

- Bringing an accursed object into one’s home would transfer the curse to the person. The principle is contamination: what is *herem* (devoted to destruction) makes anyone associated with it likewise *herem*. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- The immediate application was seen at Jericho (Joshua 6–7): Achan took devoted things and brought destruction on himself and his household. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/
- “Utterly detest” and “utterly abhor” are strong emotional terms. God’s people are not to be neutral toward idolatry; they are to share God’s own revulsion toward it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-7/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html

## SUMMARY OF DENOMINATIONAL DISTINCTIVES

| Issue | Tradition | Distinctive |
|-------|-----------|-------------|
| **Election (vv. 6–8)** | Reformed | God’s choice is unconditional, rooted solely in His free will, not in any foreseen merit in Israel. Illustrates God’s sovereign election of believers (Romans 9–11). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html |
| **Election (vv. 6–8)** | Baptist (Garner-Howes) | God’s choice based on grace, not merit, paralleling Romans 4:13; 11:6. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-7.html |
| **Separation (vv. 1–5)** | Baptist | Emphasises separation from idolatry and unequally yoked relationships as a timeless principle (2 Corinthians 6:14–18). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html |
| **Prosperity blessings (vv. 12–15)** | Word of Faith / Pentecostal charismatic | Material prosperity and physical health are covenant rights for believers who exercise faith. Deuteronomy 7:13 and the Abrahamic covenant are key proof-texts. — https://pneumareview.com/reconstructing-word-of-faith-theology/ |
| **Prosperity blessings (vv. 12–15)** | Lutheran (LCMS) | Rejects “health and wealth” interpretation. Faith is God’s gift, not a human force. NT teaches contentment, not guaranteed riches (Luke 12:15; Philippians 4:11–12). — https://files.lcms.org/api/file/preview/A810B65D-D26A-4762-8633-D85070F5E77A |
| **Prosperity blessings (vv. 12–15)** | Reformed/Baptist (Desiring God, Bible.org) | Prosperity gospel is idolatrous; Galatians 3:14 refers to spiritual blessing (the Spirit), not material wealth. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-gods-of-the-prosperity-gospel ; https://bible.org/article/bankruptcy-prosperity-gospel-exercise-biblical-and-theological-ethics |
| **Covenant conditionality (v. 12)** | Broad evangelical / Dallas Seminary | The Mosaic covenant blessings are conditional on obedience, distinct from the unconditional Abrahamic covenant. Israel’s history is read through Deuteronomy 27–29. The new covenant (Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 36) is needed because Israel could never sustain the required obedience. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/deuteronomy-7.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-7.html |

## AREAS NOT COVERED

Due to search and fetch limits, I was unable to retrieve detailed material from:

- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** Searches for newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org returned no results within the search allowance.
- **Modern scholarship:** bibleodyssey.org and full NET Bible notes (netbible.org) could not be accessed.
- **Lutheran denominational commentaries** on Deuteronomy 7 specifically (beyond the LCMS Word-Faith document).
- **Methodist/Wesleyan/Holiness** specific treatments from seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu.

These would require additional rounds of searching to fill in.
